question:
A 80-year-old male presents with progressive lower abdominal pain one day after undergoing total
knee replacement surgery for advanced degenerative osteoarthritis. The procedure was performed
under general anesthesia, and a temporary catheter was used perioperatively for fluid management.
Several hours post-surgery, he developed decreasing voiding volumes, nausea, and dull lower
abdominal pain. His medical history includes Sjögren syndrome. He is sexually active with his wife and
another partner, using condoms inconsistently. He does not smoke and drinks one to two beers on
weekends. His current medications include pilocarpine eye drops. On examination, he appears
uncomfortable and diaphoretic. Vital signs include a temperature of 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse of 81/min,
and blood pressure of 137/65 mm Hg. Abdominal examination reveals a pelvic mass extending to the
umbilicus, which is dull on percussion and diffusely tender to palpation. Laboratory results show a
hemoglobin concentration of 13.9 g/dL, leukocyte count of 9000/mm³, and platelet count of
230,000/mm³. An attempt at transurethral recatheterization is unsuccessful. What is the most likely
underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms? Answer Choices: (A) Pelvic hematoma (B) Neurogenic
bladder (C) Bladder rupture (D) Ureteral obstruction due to malignancy (E) Postoperative urinary

retention due to anesthesia (F) Acute pyelonephritis (G) Urethral stricture (H) Obstructive uropathy due
to a bladder stone (I) Acute prostatitis (J) Benign prostatic enlargement
 A. Acute prostatitis
B. Postoperative urinary retention due to anesthesia
C. Obstructive uropathy due to a bladder stone
D. Acute pyelonephritis
E. Pelvic hematoma
F. Benign prostatic enlargement
G. Bladder rupture
H. Urethral stricture
I. Ureteral obstruction due to malignancy
J. Neurogenic bladder
